When diesel is scarce and margins are strong, every planned maintenance day appears to sacrifice valuable output.

...

One large turnaround can change a regional vessel programme.

Product-tanker effects move in the opposite direction

When a refinery stops, its diesel, gasoline, jet, or naphtha exports decline.

...

Moving a turnaround can lose the original resources and create a longer future outage.
War-related aviation, customs, and supply-chain disruption can make rescheduling harder. The value of an available team belongs in the decision.

U.S. Gulf Product Tanker Earnings Surge 110% as Atlantic Freight Market Rebounds

🔔 Subscribe to ShipUniverse Weekly →
U.S. GULF & ATLANTIC PRODUCT TANKER MARKET
TC21: U.S. Gulf → Caribbean TC14: U.S. Gulf → UK-Continent
U .S. Gulf medium-range (MR) product tanker earnings rebounded sharply during the week ending November 27, 2026, according to the Baltic Exchange's latest tanker market assessment. Estimated time-charter-equivalent earnings on the U.S. Gulf–Caribbean route increased from $19,600 to $41,200 per day, while the U.S. Gulf–UK Continent benchmark climbed by $21,100 to $44,800 per day. The Baltic MR Atlantic Triangulation Basket also advanced from $36,400 to $52,300 per day, reversing part of the substantial earnings decline recorded earlier in November.

U.S. Gulf Tankers Regain Pricing Power

The recovery was particularly pronounced on the Caribbean trade. Assessed freight for a 38,000-tonne TC21 cargo increased from $750,000 to approximately $1.11 million, a gain of 48%. The resulting daily earnings improvement was proportionately larger, demonstrating the sensitivity of tanker voyage economics to changes in freight revenue after voyage expenses.
On the transatlantic TC14 route, freight increased by 101 Worldscale points to WS336. Both U.S. Gulf benchmarks are now generating estimated daily earnings above $40,000, substantially improving the commercial position of owners with vessels available in the region.

A Strong Recovery, but Still Below October Levels

The rebound follows several weeks of declining product tanker earnings. At the end of October, Caribbean MR earnings were approaching $78,000 per day, with Atlantic triangulated employment generating more than $85,000 per day. Today's improvement restores only part of those earlier gains.

Atlantic Tanker Economics Become Increasingly One-Sided

While U.S. Gulf export routes strengthened, the TC2 benchmark covering refined-product shipments from Northwest Europe to the U.S. Atlantic Coast deteriorated to just $6,600 per day.
That leaves a $38,200-per-day difference between the individual TC14 and TC2 round-trip benchmarks. Owners evaluating Atlantic employment must therefore consider vessel positioning, return cargo availability, ballast distances and overall trading-cycle economics rather than relying on the strongest individual freight assessment.
The recovery in the Atlantic triangulation benchmark suggests that combining complementary cargo legs can produce materially stronger earnings than operating on weaker standalone routes.

What Tanker Operators Should Monitor Next

U.S. Gulf Vessel Availability Prompt tonnage lists will help determine whether the recovery reflects a temporary shortage of suitably positioned vessels or more sustained market tightening.
Refined Product Export Demand U.S. Gulf refinery utilization, export cargo nominations and overseas product pricing will influence the durability of freight demand.
Atlantic Repositioning The earnings disparity between eastbound and westbound routes could encourage additional vessels to reposition toward the U.S. Gulf, eventually moderating regional freight rates.
Post-Thanksgiving Fixing Activity Early December cargo enquiries will provide a clearer indication of whether the recovery can extend beyond the U.S. holiday period.
Market Summary: The U.S. Gulf has emerged as a renewed source of strength for Atlantic MR product tankers, with Caribbean earnings more than doubling and transatlantic earnings approaching $45,000 per day. The broader Atlantic market remains uneven, however, and all three recovering benchmarks are still below their October 30 levels. December fixing activity will be important in determining whether the latest gains develop into a sustained recovery.

Oil tanker freight rates plunge in Asia as Strait of Hormuz attacks disrupt fuel shipments

OilNOW · November 19, 2026
Oil tanker freight rates across Asia-Pacific have fallen sharply as attacks on commercial vessels near the Strait of Hormuz disrupt refined fuel shipments, leaving more tankers competing for fewer cargoes.
S&P Global reported on November 18 that Medium Range (MR) tanker freight rates dropped by 125 Worldscale points on a benchmark Middle East route, as security concerns slowed vessel movements through the critical shipping passage.
“Cargo flows are limited; there are hardly any refined products coming out from the Persian Gulf. Several tankers are looking for employment and ready to snap up cargoes at lower rates,” a senior executive at a clean oil tanker company told S&P Global.
According to UK Maritime Trade Operations, three commercial vessels were attacked in the Persian Gulf and waters off Oman over two days.
Wood Mackenzie cuts Q4 global crude run forecast by 1.4 million b/d as Middle East conflict drags on
The growing risks have prompted many shipping companies to avoid the Strait, while others wait for vessels inside the Persian Gulf to transport fuel to ship-to-ship transfer locations in Oman and western India.
Daily vessel transits through Hormuz fell to just 14 on November 9, compared with 32 at the end of October, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea data. Brokers estimated that fewer than six refined-product tankers were passing through the Strait on an average day.
The disruption is already affecting freight negotiations.
Brokers reported that Vitol provisionally booked the Torm Stellar at Worldscale 500 for November 25 diesel loading on the Duqm-East Africa route. Another tanker, Weco Amalie, was subsequently placed at Worldscale 475 for the Sikka-East Africa route, representing a decline of 125 points from the previous comparable fixture.
Iran says U.S. failing to meet conditions for reopening of Hormuz Strait
The weakness has spread to North Asia, where refined-product exports from China have fallen short of expectations despite the government announcing approximately 5.65 million metric tons of additional export quotas in late October.
On the South Korea-Japan route, the Oriental Sunstone was provisionally booked for US$975,000, marking the first reported fixture below US$1 million since late August.
Lower MR freight rates are also prompting some charterers to consider splitting larger fuel shipments into smaller parcels rather than using Long Range (LR) tankers.

Trade volumes are stalling, fleet capacity keeps arriving and longer voyages are concealing the mismatch. The next rate cycle may be decided by what happens to the ships already afloat.

Shipowners may enter 2027 with a dangerously misleading signal: the world's merchant fleet can be busy even when the world is shipping no additional cargo. UNCTAD forecasts zero growth in seaborne tonnage in 2026, but an increase in the miles that cargo travels. Diversions, congestion, sanctions and restricted passage absorb vessel-days, lifting freight rates while the underlying fleet continues growing. The commercial question is how much of that demand survives when routes shorten, ships return and newbuildings enter service.

By Mukesh Sahdev Visit author profile

The growing exposure of shuttle tankers to attacks in the Gulf is reshaping global VLCC deployment, ship-to-ship transfer economics and freight pricing. With nearly 20% of the shuttle tanker fleet having been struck and Atlantic VLCC liftings recovering by 40% week-on-week, the market faces a renewed redistribution of tanker capacity. XA sees ......

What this insight covers

VORTEXA's released latest Global Freight Snapshot report with a spotlight on efficiency of tanker strikes on shuttle transits, and the marginal recovery of VLCC Atlantic liftings in the context of reduced Hormuz transits.
* Shuttle tankers are becoming disproportionately exposed to attacks. Around 40% of Gulf strikes now involve shuttle tankers, compared with approximately 14% before September. Of the 174 shuttle tankers identified, 34 have been struck, representing nearly 20% of the fleet.
* STS operations have reduced effective global tanker capacity. The increased reliance on ship-to-ship transfers, shuttle voyages and associated waiting times has increased the vessel-days required to move the same volume of crude.
* The Gulf's dependence on STS operations has increased significantly. Around 60% of Gulf exports in September and October reportedly moved through six relay zones, compared with just 7% in March.
* The balance between STS and non-STS flows is changing again. Escalating attacks in October have coincided with declining Middle East Gulf (MEG) STS flows and recovering non-STS flows.
* Atlantic crude sourcing is regaining momentum. Atlantic VLCC liftings increased 40% week-on-week in the week ending 22 November, although major supply regions remain below their post-war peaks.
* TD3C and TD22 are rising for potentially different reasons. Both routes are up approximately 14% week-on-week, but TD3C appears supported by tightening vessel availability, while TD22 is recovering from depressed levels.
* The next freight move will depend on vessel redistribution rather than crude volumes alone. The relative pace of tanker repositioning, replacement demand for shuttle vessels and Asian crude purchasing will determine regional freight direction.

Frontline Lands Reported $24 Million VLCC Fixture as Tanker Owners Hold Out for Higher Rates

🔔 Subscribe to ShipUniverse Weekly →
📍 Middle East Gulf — Global VLCC Freight Market
The Middle East Gulf remains a major center of VLCC employment and elevated crude tanker freight rates. The map provides wider market context; the loading and discharge locations of Frontline's reported fixture have not been independently verified.
F rontline has reportedly secured a very large crude carrier (VLCC) fixture valued at approximately $24 million, according to November 27 reporting by TradeWinds. The fixture comes amid renewed pressure on tanker earnings and disagreements between vessel owners and charterers over freight rates, while the Middle East market remains comparatively firm. The report follows Frontline's November 20 financial results, in which the company disclosed record forward spot bookings across all three of its tanker segments, including contracted fourth-quarter VLCC earnings averaging $562,600 per day on 68% of available spot days. The specific voyage costs and net earnings associated with the reported $24 million fixture remain unverified.

Frontline's Exposure to an Extraordinary Tanker Market

The reported $24 million fixture comes just one week after Frontline disclosed an unprecedented increase in contracted fourth-quarter spot earnings. Its VLCC bookings are averaging nearly four times the daily earnings achieved during the third quarter.
The company's November 20 results provide a clearer measure of the financial environment in which the latest fixture was negotiated.
Frontline Tanker Earnings — Q3 vs. Q4 Bookings
* Vessel Segment | Q3 2026 Actual Spot TCE | Q4 Contracted Spot TCE | Increase | Q4 Spot Days Covered
* VLCC | $148,500/day | $562,600/day | +279% | 68%
* Suezmax | $102,500/day | $324,300/day | +216% | 69%
* LR2 / Aframax | $67,800/day | $190,800/day | +181% | 68%
Q4 figures represent contracted earnings disclosed on November 20, not completed quarterly results. Frontline expects realized fourth-quarter spot TCEs to be lower because of ballast days.
23.3 Times Cash Breakeven
Frontline's contracted fourth-quarter VLCC spot TCE of $562,600 per day is approximately 23.3 times its estimated daily VLCC cash breakeven of $24,100. This comparison illustrates the scale of current earnings potential, rather than the actual profit margin of an individual fixture.

One Tanker Market, Very Different Earnings

The latest Baltic Exchange figures reveal a substantial disparity between Middle East Gulf tanker earnings and other major crude export routes. Although Atlantic rates have experienced periods of recovery, the premium attached to Middle East Gulf employment remains exceptional.

Standardized benchmark estimates, not guaranteed vessel earnings. Actual returns depend on vessel specifications, voyage expenses, positioning, contractual terms and operating conditions.
The Middle East Gulf–China benchmark is currently generating estimated daily returns more than four times those of the U.S. Gulf–China route. For vessel owners, however, the higher Middle East rates must be evaluated alongside security exposure, insurance costs, crew safety and potential delays.

What Could a $24 Million Fixture Generate?

A fixture's headline value does not establish its profitability. If the reported $24 million represents gross voyage freight, the resulting TCE would depend heavily on voyage duration, repositioning requirements and the expenses incurred in completing the contract.
Illustrative $24 Million Voyage Economics

...

Owners — Protecting Earnings
High alternative employment rates strengthen owners' ability to reject weaker offers, particularly when vessel availability is limited for specific loading windows.
Charterers — Resisting Premiums
Additional vessel availability and expensive crude transportation encourage charterers to delay commitments or renegotiate freight where cargo schedules permit.
Atlantic Basin — Uneven Demand
Western crude export routes remain commercially attractive, but their earnings are substantially below the Middle East Gulf benchmark.
Oil Markets — Higher Delivered Costs
Expensive tanker transportation can narrow crude trading margins, alter refinery purchasing decisions and reduce the attractiveness of certain long-haul cargoes.

Frontline Is Balancing Spot Exposure With Long-Term Cover

Frontline reported third-quarter profit of $641.4 million and expects its fleet to reach 77 vessels, including 40 VLCCs, following delivery of its remaining newbuilding in early 2027.
As of November 20, the company had 15 VLCCs committed to time charters with initial durations exceeding one year. Four recently delivered VLCC newbuildings were secured on one-year contracts paying between $110,000 and $120,000 per day.
This combination provides contracted revenue while retaining exposure to unusually strong spot market conditions. It also offers some protection against the rapid freight corrections that can follow a normalization of oil trade routes.
The Next Market Test
The durability of current VLCC earnings will depend on December cargo nominations, Middle East security conditions, regional vessel availability and the pace at which charterers accept elevated freight offers. Repeated fixtures at comparable levels would provide stronger evidence of sustained pricing power than any individual transaction.
Frontline's reported $24 million fixture reflects the exceptional contract values available in today's crude tanker market. However, substantial regional earnings differences, increasing vessel availability and uncertainty surrounding individual voyage expenses remain important factors in determining whether these extraordinary revenue opportunities translate into sustained fleet profitability.

The Defense Logistics Agency strengthened domestic industrial capacity and supported national security priorities by committing $2 billion to acquire strategic and critical materials during fiscal year 2026. As the organization responsible for supporting the stockpile, DLA Strategic Materials improved access to materials important to the nation's industrial readiness, said Eric Mata, DLA Strategic Materials director.
The national defense stockpile reduces the risk of material shortages that could affect national defense and essential civilian industries. Strategic and critical materials are those needed to meet military, industrial, and essential civilian requirements during a national emergency, but aren't available commercially in sufficient quantities to meet those needs.
Most of the critical mineral contracts awarded through DLA 's Contracting Services Office were targeted demand signals to enable domestic production and to support the National Defense Strategy emphasis on resilient, secure supply chains, Mata says.
"Domestic sourcing is especially important when a material is essential to national defense, is subject to concentrated or vulnerable supply chains, is difficult to replace, and is not readily available from reliable sources in the quantities or forms required," Mata explains. "In those cases, domestic acquisition and stockpiling can help reduce single-point-of-failure risks, sustain U.S. industrial capability and preserve material availability during disruption."
Materials sourced for the stockpile can range from high-purity aluminum to vanadium pentoxide, with many elements, metals, and compounds in between. In addition to mining, approaches like recovery, recycling, refining, and processing can also produce these materials. Where technically and economically feasible, domestic reclamation strengthens supply resilience by providing secondary sources of critical materials, Mata says.
The National Defense Strategy calls for supporting the defense industrial base through reshoring strategic industries and expanding domestic production.
DLA’s acquisitions for the national defense stockpile direct demand toward American material suppliers and processors, strengthening industrial readiness and resilience, Mata says.
“These materials support a range of industrial capabilities across aerospace, maritime, ground, space, communications and munitions-related sectors,” he says.
Stockpiled materials reduce uncertainty for the defense industrial base and provide demand signals that help sustain specialized capabilities, Mata said. They work alongside other War Department and federal projects to strengthen domestic critical-material supply chains to complement — rather than replace — other investment options.
He also notes the national security benefits of stockpiling reduce exposure to foreign supply risk by lowering reliance on overseas producers, long transportation routes and geographically concentrated supply chains.
“These efforts are helping domestic companies plan production, retain skilled workers and expand capacity where economically viable,” Mata says. “By pairing targeted acquisitions with domestic sourcing and broader industrial-base investments, DLA Strategic Materials is helping build a more resilient supply chain for materials important to national defense.”

The US Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) awarded up to $3.3bn in firm, fixed-price indefinite quantity/indefinite delivery (IDIQ) contracts for cobalt, gallium, nickel and high purity aluminum for the national defense stockpile, prompting questions over the quantities to actually be purchased.
Under an IDIQ contract, the agency may place purchases during the established ordering period under a maximum total purchasing amount, although the agency is not obligated to buy that volume or value. The awarded values represent ceilings of what could be spent under the IDIQ contracts and are not guaranteed purchases.
None of the acquisitions were announced officially by the awardee companies, but a spokesperson for the DLA noted awardees can choose to publicly share deals. Since the beginning of 2025 Metallus , Elmet , Largo , US Antimony and Global Advanced Metals all shared public updates on awards with the agency for strategic materials.
The DLA committed $2bn to acquiring strategic and critical materials for the national defense stockpile throughout fiscal year 2026 (1 October 2025 to 30 September 2026), including high purity aluminum, according to an agency press release.
Previously, the DLA would release the Annual Materials Plan (AMP), a list of potential material acquisitions including maximum quantities to be purchased, at the beginning of the agency's fiscal year in October. The DLA never released an AMP for the 2026 fiscal year and has yet to release one for 2027, leaving market participants still mulling which materials the agency already secured and what will be prioritized.

US reports $2B in mineral stockpile commitments

By: Staff Writer November 9, 2026
The U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) says it committed $2 billion (C$2.8 billion) to acquire strategic and critical materials for the National Defense Stockpile during fiscal 2026, which ended Sept. 30.
The agency disclosed the total in a Nov. 5 announcement but did not identify the contracts, suppliers or quantities involved, or say how much had been paid out or delivered.
“These efforts are helping domestic companies plan production, retain skilled workers and expand capacity where economically viable,” DLA Strategic Materials director Eric Mata said in the release.
The fiscal-year tally updates Washington’s efforts to turn government buying power into reliable mineral supplies. DLA’s lithium tender delays in July highlighted the difficulty of converting purchasing plans into physical material, even as the government seeks to reduce dependence on foreign sources.

Existing commitments

The Pentagon’s stockpiling campaign was already under way in October 2025, when it moved to acquire up to $1 billion of critical minerals, the Financial Times reported.
Congress provided $2 billion for the stockpile through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in July 2025, with the money available through fiscal 2029. In its April budget submission , DLA said authority to use that appropriation came in fiscal 2026.
DLA did not explain how the latest total relates to that funding or to previously announced contracts.
For example, The Elmet Group (Nasdaq: ELMT) announced a tungsten supply contract in September with a ceiling of $2 billion and a guaranteed minimum commitment of $150 million. The company said deliveries would wait until additional supply became available. That contract ceiling cannot be treated as another $2 billion of committed spending.
The defence stockpile is also separate from Project Vault , the reserve for manufacturers backed by Export-Import Bank of the United States financing. Project Vault was preparing to offer up to $1 billion in loans to manufacturers in October.

Domestic supply

The National Defense Stockpile holds materials for military and essential civilian needs during national emergencies, when commercial supplies may fall short. Most of DLA’s critical mineral contracts were intended to encourage domestic production, Mata said.
Materials sourced for the stockpile can range from high-purity aluminum to vanadium pentoxide, DLA said, without identifying the materials covered by the latest total. Recovery and recycling can provide additional domestic sources where technically and economically feasible, Mata said.
“Domestic sourcing is especially important when a material is essential to national defense, is subject to concentrated or vulnerable supply chains, is difficult to replace, and is not readily available from reliable sources in the quantities or forms required,” Mata said. “In those cases, domestic acquisition and stockpiling can help reduce single-point-of-failure risks, sustain U.S. industrial capability, and preserve material availability during disruption.”

US DLA Awards Up to $3.3bn in Critical Minerals Supply Deals for National Defense Stockpile

Published: Nov 12, 2026 11:18 Source: SteelHome Share   
The United States Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) has awarded contracts worth up to approximately $3.3 billion for the potential acquisition of cobalt, nickel, gallium and high-purity aluminum for the national defense stockpile, as Washington seeks to strengthen strategic mineral reserves and secure supplies of materials critical to defense manufacturing.
The contracts, awarded to Glencore, Rio Tinto, Arconic and Atlantic Alumina, cover purchasing arrangements extending over five years. However, the agreements are structured as firm-fixed-price, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) contracts, meaning the announced values represent maximum purchasing limits rather than guaranteed expenditures or confirmed material deliveries.
Under this contracting mechanism, the DLA can place orders during the agreed period, subject to the contractual ceilings, but is not required to purchase the maximum quantities or spend the full authorized amounts. Consequently, the awards do not establish how much material will ultimately enter the US national defense stockpile.
The distinction has attracted attention from metals market participants, particularly because the DLA has not disclosed complete purchasing quantities, material specifications or delivery schedules for several of the contracts.

...

Rio Tinto and Arconic Receive High-Purity Aluminum Awards
High-purity aluminum accounts for the largest combined value among the disclosed contracts, with Rio Tinto and Arconic each receiving awards worth up to $995 million.
The US Department of Defense announced Rio Tinto's award on September 25, noting that the procurement had been conducted competitively and attracted three responses.
Rio Tinto confirmed that it would supply a small volume of high-purity aluminum but did not disclose the expected quantity or detailed delivery schedule. The five-year contract's maximum value therefore should not be interpreted as a confirmed purchase of nearly $1 billion in aluminum.
US aluminum producer Arconic also received a five-year IDIQ contract with a maximum value of $995 million. The company did not provide additional information on the award.
Arconic has previously received US defense funding to expand high-purity aluminum production. In 2023, the Department of Defense awarded the company $45.5 million to support production capacity for aluminum used in missiles and munitions.
The latest procurement awards reflect continued US efforts to strengthen access to specialized aluminum materials required for defense-related applications.
Atlantic Alumina Awarded Up to $350 Million for Gallium
Louisiana-based alumina producer Atlantic Alumina, also known as Atalco, has secured a five-year contract worth up to $350 million to supply gallium to the DLA.
The agreement covers a potential quantity of 55,610 kilograms, equivalent to approximately 55.6 tonnes, of gallium. As with the other IDIQ contracts, the specified amount represents the scope of the purchasing arrangement rather than a guarantee that the full quantity will be ordered.
Gallium is an important input for semiconductor manufacturing, making it a strategic material for electronics and defense-related supply chains.
The Department of Defense has also invested $400 million in Atlantic Alumina, with part of the equity financing intended to support the expansion of primary gallium production.
Once commercial operations begin, the company expects to establish annual gallium production capacity of approximately 50 tonnes. The production initiative and the DLA supply agreement represent separate but related elements of US efforts to develop domestic gallium supply.
Lack of Annual Materials Plans Adds Uncertainty to Procurement Outlook
The latest contracts come as the DLA continues to expand its strategic materials procurement activities.
The agency previously announced a $2 billion commitment to acquiring strategic and critical materials for the national defense stockpile during fiscal year 2026, which ran from October 1, 2025, through September 30, 2026. High-purity aluminum was among the materials identified for procurement.
Historically, the DLA published an Annual Materials Plan (AMP) at the beginning of each fiscal year, outlining potential acquisitions and maximum quantities under consideration. However, the agency did not publish an AMP for fiscal year 2026 and has not yet released one for fiscal year 2027.
The absence of these plans has made it more difficult for market participants to determine which materials the government has already secured and which commodities may receive priority in future procurement programmes.
Although several companies, including Metallus, Elmet, Largo, US Antimony and Global Advanced Metals, have publicly disclosed strategic materials contracts with the DLA since early 2025, the recipients of the latest cobalt, nickel, aluminum and gallium awards did not independently announce all of the agreements.
The DLA has indicated that contract recipients may choose whether to disclose their awards publicly.
Overall, the approximately $3.3 billion in disclosed contract ceilings highlights the scale of potential US defense stockpile procurement across several critical mineral markets. Nevertheless, the actual effect on supply, prices and inventory accumulation will depend on the quantities ordered, delivery schedules and whether suppliers source material from existing inventories or additional production.
For cobalt and gallium in particular, the timing and scale of government purchases will be important factors in determining whether the contracts create additional market demand. Until the DLA provides further procurement details, the announced contract values should be viewed as purchasing authorizations rather than confirmed stockpile additions.

European Defence Agency says EU ministers endorsed eight cooperation opportunities spanning missiles and strategic enablers

By Martin Chomsky (Defence Industry Europe)
EU | November 23, 2026
European Defence Agency says EU ministers endorsed eight cooperation opportunities spanning missiles and strategic enablers
Photo: European Defence Agency (EDA).
EU defence ministers have endorsed eight opportunities for military cooperation in a review that urges governments to plan capabilities together before taking national procurement decisions. The 2026 Coordinated Annual Review on Defence (CARD), approved on 17 November, identifies opportunities ranging from missiles and unmanned systems to the infrastructure needed to sustain European operations.
The report finds that agreement on defence priorities has not yet translated into a consistently collaborative approach to purchasing equipment. It recommends considering cooperation at the capability planning stage and incorporating it into national programmes and budgets, with projects prepared to draw on EU funding.
Ministers endorsed opportunities to cooperate on a family of cruise missiles, long-range artillery using multiple launch rocket systems and a family of long-range air defence interceptors. They also backed opportunities involving modular, interoperable unmanned ground vehicles and layered counter-drone systems for force protection and critical infrastructure.
The other three opportunities concern space-based early warning, detection and tracking, a European secure defence cloud and a European approach to strategic air mobility. The European Defence Agency (EDA) identifies these as strategic enablers that allow Europe to decide, act and sustain operations autonomously.
“With CARD, we have identified three collaborative opportunities related to strategic enablers,” said EDA Chief Executive André Denk. “From space-based early warning to strategic air mobility, and a secure, federated defence cloud architecture, these strategic enablers are essential to strengthening Europe’s deterrence and defence capabilities.”
Their scale, cost and dependence on shared architectures and networks make cooperation necessary, the report says. It argues that no single country can develop and support them alone, while access cannot be assumed in every future contingency.
CARD calls for further analysis, stronger member-state involvement and dedicated roadmaps for these capabilities. That work should build on EDA’s activities and Priority Capability Areas, in coherence with NATO.
The report makes five recommendations covering earlier cooperation, planning beyond 2030, joint work on strategic enablers, the full process of capability development and faster adoption of innovation. It stresses that buying equipment is only part of delivering forces that can deploy and operate effectively.
Personnel, training, doctrine, logistics, sustainment and interoperability increasingly determine how much defence investment becomes usable capability. Shared training capacity, common information-sharing architectures and integration of sensors with command and control offer opportunities that can be delivered faster than large programmes.
The review also identifies delays between promising technological results and operational use. It attributes those delays to experimentation, requirements and acquisition being managed too sequentially and calls for innovation to reach the field faster.
Immediate readiness requirements must be balanced with investment in medium- and long-term needs beyond 2030. The report warns that underinvestment may become visible only after several planning cycles, when correcting it would take considerable time and money.
More systematic cooperation would give manufacturers clearer and more predictable demand, supporting production at scale and reducing supply-chain dependencies. Delivering that cooperation also requires stronger intergovernmental support for joint acquisition, capability development and research.
EDA’s strengthening process is intended to provide that support and help CARD and Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO) deliver results. EU incentives, including the European Defence Industry Programme, would support those efforts.
At the 17 November EDA Steering Board, ministers also endorsed a joint statement on defence security of supply. They agreed to increase the agency’s budget.
EDA prepared the report in coordination with the European External Action Service and the EU Military Staff. It is the final deliverable of the fourth CARD cycle, covering 2025–2026.

Europe is building drone defenses. But can it make them work together?

European governments are spending billions to protect their skies. Turning those national investments into a coherent defense capability may prove more difficult.
Illustrative image of a soldier retrieving an Anafi USA drone during a live-fire exercise at Novo Selo Training Area, Bulgaria, 7 August 2025. (J Marshall/Tribaleye Images)
By Paula Soler
Paula Soler is a reporter at The Parliament Magazine
25 Nov 2026
@pausoler98
Share this page
   ?subject=Europe+is+building+drone+defenses.+But+can+it+make+them+work+together%3f&body=theparliamentmagazine.eu%2fnews%2farticle%2feurope-is-building-drone-defenses-but-can-it-make-them-work-together 
Europe's skies have become increasingly difficult to defend. Drones have disrupted airports, appeared over military installations and exposed weaknesses in air defenses designed for a different era. At least 144 drone incidents were reported across the European Union between August 2024 and February 2026, according to a report from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In response, Brussels put forward plans for a "drone wall" in 2025. A year later, the rebranded European Drone Defence Initiative , the multilayered system for detecting, neutralizing and striking dronesis due to reach initial capacity by the end of December and become fully operational a year later.
Much of the work is taking place at the national level.

...

Turning innovation into contracts

Europe's drone industry has a familiar defense problem: demand for its products is soaring, but orders are not coming fast enough.
EU countries plan to invest €18.9 billion in drone technologies between 2024 and 2029, according to a leaked report by the European Defence Agency . Yet only a third of planned counter-drone and very short-range air defense programs are expected to be delivered by the end of the decade.
In an industry where technology can become obsolete within months, Europe's lengthy procurement procedures risk leaving armed forces with equipment that is already outdated by the time it enters service.
"Procurement is not materializing at a pace that matches the urgency," said Arthur de Liedekerke, a partner and senior director at political consultancy Rasmussen Global.
The government departments responsible for buying military equipment have not necessarily expanded alongside defense budgets, he said, while decades of working with established manufacturers have made it difficult for smaller, more innovative companies to break into the market.
"We need shorter procurement cycles, operational testing with end users and contracts that allow frequent upgrades," he said.
Some manufacturers are already benefiting from Europe's military spending spree.

...

But governments that develop their drone defenses in isolation risk investing in overlapping technologies, deploying systems that cannot exchange data and creating legal uncertainty over when and by whom drones can be intercepted, defense experts say.
“To ensure coherence and interoperability, especially at the data-exchange level, more coordination needs to happen now,” Ulrike Franke, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, a pan-European think tank, wrote in an August analysis .
There is also the question of how much Europe can afford to spend defending its skies.

...

Where national interests collide

Disagreements over what constitutes the bigger threat make protecting European airspace even harder.
For governments on NATO's eastern flank, drones are part of a broader military threat from Russia. Further west, much of the concern centers on how vulnerable airports, ports and other sensitive sites are to disruption, espionage and sabotage.

EDA says six EU countries explore joint purchase of CBRN surveillance equipment and services

By Defence Industry Europe (newsroom)
EU | November 21, 2026
EDA says six EU countries explore joint purchase of CBRN surveillance equipment and services
Photo: European Defence Agency (EDA).
Austria, Croatia, Germany, Lithuania, Slovakia and Slovenia are exploring a joint purchase of chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear surveillance equipment and services, the European Defence Agency said. Any procurement would remain subject to national approval procedures.
The six countries signed a declaration of political intent on 17 November 2026 alongside EDA’s Ministerial Steering Board meeting. It opens the way to possible common procurement under the next phase of the CBRN Surveillance as a Service project, with development expected to finish in mid-2027.
EDA’s new Collaborative Defence Procurement Centre, or CDPC, will support the initiative by helping the countries combine requirements and coordinate purchases. Other EU member states will be invited to take part.
“European defence readiness requires more than ambition. It requires delivering concrete capabilities together,” said EDA Chief Executive André Denk.
“Through its new Collaborative Defence Procurement Centre, EDA can help Member States combine their purchasing power, coordinate joint procurement, reduce costs and deliver interoperable solutions. This is how EDA turns European defence cooperation into concrete results,” Denk said.
Austria leads the project, which builds on cooperation launched in 2018 under Permanent Structured Cooperation, or PESCO, with EDA support. National experts, innovators and industry have worked together on technologies intended to improve CBRN reconnaissance and surveillance.
These include sensors that detect hazardous chemical, biological and radiological substances and transmit information about them. Mounted on drones or autonomous ground vehicles, the sensors allow forces to investigate threats while reducing the risk of exposing personnel.
Specially developed software immediately processes the transmitted data and produces a real-time CBRN situational picture to support commanders’ decisions. Some of the technologies were recently tested during the EU Operational Experimentation exercise in Portugal, demonstrating their potential for operational use.
“The countries that acquire the CBRN reconnaissance and surveillance systems under this project can easily cooperate with the systems of other participating countries. Threats can be detected without putting human lives at risk,” said Austrian Defence Minister Klaudia Tanner.
The declaration follows defence ministers’ September 2026 approval of a stronger EDA role in capability development, innovation and collaborative procurement. That decision included establishing the CDPC to help governments pool requirements and buy services and off-the-shelf solutions together.
The planned purchase would give participants interoperable systems and services, with combined demand offering economies of scale and a lower administrative burden. EDA said the initiative illustrated how collaborative development could lead to joint acquisition, supporting the broader objective of European defence readiness by 2030.

Sovereignty is here to stay in space defence spending

November 2026

Alexander Clark

Governments worldwide are increasing their spending on space-based defence capabilities as geopolitical fragmentation forces them to seek sovereign control over their assets. NATO members and partner countries 1 have awarded over USD51 billion in total contract value on space-based defence in 2026, up from USD20 billion in 2025. 2 Early investment this year included procurement of satellite communications (satcom) and Earth observation satellites for secure, reliable access to data and networks. However, the largest portion of spending has gone to missile early warning (MEW) and space domain awareness (SDA) as governments and militaries work to expand monitoring capabilities and increasingly leverage space for defence purposes.
Sovereignty will remain a dominant theme in space spending through 2027 and beyond, and this presents an opportunity for vendors selling in national markets. 3 However, the trend will challenge vendors seeking to sell internationally, especially given changes in government, delays in space defence programmes and distinct national preferences.

The US Golden Dome initiative is powering sovereign spending on MEW

...

The Franco-German Joint Early Warning for a European Lookout (JEWEL) programme, as part of the EU ‘Odin’s Eye’ project, is the prominent effort in Europe. However, no public contract announcements have followed the programme’s inception in 2025. This reflects how, despite growing interest and investment,
1 NATO partner countries include Australia, Colombia, Iraq, Japan, Mongolia, New Zealand, Pakistan and South Korea.
2 See Analysys Mason’s Defence and civil government spending in space database .
3 See Analysys Mason’s Sovereignty in space report.
Sovereignty is here to stay in space defence spending | 2
MEW is still a new market.

...

SDA is an emerging opportunity, but sovereignty will limit vendors’ reach

SDA spending grew massively in 2026 (Figure 2) as nations prioritised the protection of sovereign assets and hostile acts against satellites increased. Spending will continue to grow while geopolitical tensions remain acute, creating demand for SDA satellites and associated technology.

...

Vendors, in turn, are likely to be limited to supplying hardware and other core technologies. Nonetheless, as hostile actors increasingly target commercial satellites that support defence, the operators that vendors partner with could become customers of SDA services.
Figure 2: NATO year-on-year spending on SDA in the public domain, by segment

Countries looking to reduce their reliance on foreign providers are fuelling a surge in sovereign satcom spending

The value of awarded satcom contracts rose from USD8 billion in 2025 to USD30 billion in 2026, driven mainly by European demand for sovereign assets (Figure 3). These amounts exclude IRIS 2 because it is primarily a civilian constellation, even though it is also used for military purposes. The flagship European defence satcom effort behind the increase in spending is Germany’s USD9.2 billion SATCOMBw4 programme, which aims to develop a constellation of up to 100 low- Earth orbit (LEO) satellites. There are signs that European countries may shift away from IRIS 2 for military satcom, and towards sovereign assets for primary capabilities. The ICEYE–Nokia partnership and France’s interim service contracts with Eutelsat indicate this shift, representing
Sovereignty is here to stay in space defence spending | 4
activity beyond IRIS 2 . Outside Europe, the USA continues to issue satcom service contracts alongside Golden Dome-related satcom elements. Canada is pursuing the Enhanced Satellite Communications Project – Polar (ESCP-P), while Australia has restarted SPA9102. Japan has also started its Next Generation Defence Satellite Communication System.
Figure 3: NATO-awarded satellite contracts in the public domain, procurement versus services
Satcom is one of the major sovereign requirements and will continue to be so.

...

Vendors are increasingly finding that robust anti-jamming and spoofing capabilities are a requirement for success, and service providers increasingly must add explicit service-continuity commitments in their service-level agreements (SLAs). These include commitments such as guaranteed minimum capacity, levels of prioritisation (for example, government traffic receiving priority during surge events in a crisis) and no shutdown of service access clauses.
Sovereignty will remain a crucial aspect of satcom satellite procurement in 2027, especially in Europe. Countries will continue to demand greater control over essential space capabilities and seek to reduce their reliance on foreign providers. Political change in the USA and elsewhere will not necessarily ease sovereignty-related procurement requirements. Vendors can expect procurement processes to increasingly favour domestic and regional suppliers, alongside industrial offsets. 5 Sovereignty is now a condition of market entry, and vendors that weigh the real profitability of each opportunity against its access requirements will be the ones that win.
5 Industrial offsets are where a national government requires a foreign company to provide certain economic benefits to the nation.

European ministers approve eight opportunities for cooperation

Brussels, 17/11/2026 (Agence Europe)
At a Steering Board of the European Defence Agency (EDA) meeting on Tuesday 17 November, European defence ministers approved eight opportunities for cooperation identified in the ‘ CARD 2026 ’ report.
These include cruise missiles, long-range artillery (multiple-launch rocket systems), modular and interoperable unmanned ground vehicles, layered counter-drone systems to protect critical infrastructure and forces, and families of long-range air-defence interceptors. Three strategic enablers were also approved: space-based early warning, detection, and tracking; the secure European defence ' cloud '; and a European approach to strategic air mobility.
The ‘ CARD 2026 ’ report, which was also approved, sets out five recommendations. According to the report, cooperation should be considered as early as possible. While Member States increasingly agree on priorities, “ cooperation continues to be pursued on an ad hoc basis after national decisions are taken ”, the EDA regrets, calling for cooperation to be built into national programmes and budgets, and for projects eligible for EU funding to be prepared.
The report also calls for planning beyond 2030, which is the date set for defence readiness.

...

The ministers also approved a joint declaration on security of supply in defence, stressing that concerted action is needed to reduce undesirable dependencies.
The declaration highlights the need to systematically take defence requirements into consideration in relevant EU initiatives and, where supply is constrained, to ensure that essential defence needs are properly protected and supported.
The ministers also believe that industry needs to take more responsibility for the resilience of its supply chains, and strengthen security of supply. “ EDTIB-based entities and their suppliers should assess and mitigate their exposure to supply chain risks, including through supplier diversification, appropriate redundancy, strategic stockpiling where necessary, and investment in substitutes where technically and economically viable ”, the declaration states.

Arabian Drilling, Saudi Arabia.

By The Edge Research Team
The Takeaway: Arabian Drilling’s SAR 1.5 billion Khafji contract is expected to add to its results from each vessel’s start date, the company said. Its release of 8 November, before the signing, reported record contracted work still to come of SAR 17.6 billion, and the filing does not say how the contract changes that figure. The filing gives no split of value between the vessels and no profit estimate.

Khafji Joint Operations (KJO) has contracted Arabian Drilling to provide and operate two self-propelled offshore service vessels in a SAR 1.5 billion deal, replacing existing contracted service for two vessels.
Arabian Drilling (2381) disclosed the contract to the Saudi Exchange on 22 November. It was published at 05:03 GMT. The filing dates both the award and the signing 19 November, three days earlier, and lists no related parties.

Two vessels, two terms

The contract covers the provision and operation of the two vessels for KJO. They are self-propelled, meaning they move under their own power, and the filing does not say what work they will do. The first is contracted for 10 years and the second for 15. The company expects the first to begin operating in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the second in the fourth quarter of 2028, and it expects the contract to contribute to its results from each start date.
Contract terms by vessel, as disclosed
* Vessel | Term | Expected start
* First | 10 years | Q4 2026
* Second | 15 years | Q4 2028
The filing gives the total value, SAR 1.5 billion, and no value for each vessel.
The filing does not say whether each term runs from the vessel’s start date, from signing or from another date, so end dates cannot be set from it.
Spread evenly over the 25 vessel-years in the two terms, the contract averages SAR 60 million per vessel-year.
That is $16 million at the riyal’s peg of 3.75 to the dollar. The Edge calculated these averages from the filed total. The filing prints no value for each vessel, and unequal rates would change them.
At equal rates, the two vessels would together average SAR 120 million a year once both are running, which the filing expects from the fourth quarter of 2028. The first vessel alone would average SAR 60 million. The release does not say which segment would report the vessels, and they replace existing contracted service, so the value is not all new revenue.

The contract replaces existing vessel service, and the filing’s two texts differ

The English text says the new contract “replaces two existing offshore service vessel contracts”. The Arabic text reads «يحل محل عقد منصتي خدمات بحرية قائمتين», which is one contract covering two existing platforms, and it uses «منصتي» for the new vessels too. The exchange page gives both texts the same date and time, so it does not show which came first.
The Arabic financial-impact line says the contract is expected to contribute to strengthening («تعزيز») the company’s results. Neither text names the counterparty of what is replaced, or gives its value or remaining terms. The filing therefore does not show how much of the contract is additional to what the vessels already earn.

The backlog the company has printed since September

...

It credits two gas awards on land and what it calls the KJO Dorra award covering four offshore rigs. The company’s filings do not use the name Dorra. The match with the 29 September award, on customer and rig count, is The Edge’s reading.
Arabian Drilling contract awards disclosed since 31 August 2026
* Disclosed | Scope | Term | Value as filed
* 31 Aug | SLB, 11 land rigs, gas | 5 years | About SAR 3 billion
* 14 Sep | SLB, 8 land rigs, gas | 5 years | About SAR 2 billion
* 29 Sep | KJO, 4 jack-up rigs | 4 years | About SAR 2 billion
* 22 Nov | KJO, 2 service vessels | 10 and 15 years | SAR 1.5 billion
Jack-up rigs are offshore drilling rigs that stand on the seabed. Values are the filings’ own; the first three are stated as approximate.
Two of these four are not new equipment. The 11 land rigs are the incumbent units under the company’s previous gas contract with SLB, and the 8 are redeployed from the existing fleet.

...

Land gross profit rose from SAR 80.5 million to SAR 96.7 million. The rise is SAR 16.2 million.
On 12 August the company said it had notice to resume its remaining suspended offshore rigs, and that it expected offshore fleet utilization to reach 100% by the end of the third quarter. The release gives no offshore utilization figure.

What the company says next

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise by approximately 8% to 10% on the third quarter, mainly from the start-up of the gas LSTK and KJO Dorra projects it was awarded. LSTK is the label the filings give the SLB gas work.
That range works out to SAR 876 million to SAR 892 million. The release predates the signing of the vessel contract and does not mention it.
It also raised its 2026 capital spending guidance to SAR 750 million to SAR 800 million, to ready rigs for contracted start dates. The earlier guidance was approximately SAR 700 million.

What the filing leaves out

The filing carries no revenue or profit estimate and no day rates. It does not describe the work the vessels do, name the counterparty of what is being replaced, give its value or end dates, or state any backlog figure.
What to watch: The filing expects the first vessel to begin operating in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the second in the fourth quarter of 2028.

Backlog, results, segment, fleet, guidance and quotation figures are from the company’s nine-month results announcement and earnings release of 8 November 2026 and its announcements of 12 August, 31 August, 14 September and 29 September.
The per-vessel-year averages, the dollar equivalent at the riyal’s peg of SAR 3.75, the per-unit-year values and the fourth-quarter revenue range are The Edge’s calculations.

Saipem Wins $650 Million Aramco Offshore Contracts in Saudi Arabia

Saipem Wins $650 Million Aramco Offshore Contracts in Saudi Arabia
Guest Contributor
Guest Contributor
Contributor
Nov 25, 2026 UpdatedNov 25, 2026 8 min read
Saipem has won two offshore contracts from Aramco in Saudi Arabia, worth about US$650 million combined. Under the awards, Saipem will engineer, build and install seven production deck manifolds, about 39 km of pipeline and about 41 km of power cable. The work spans five of the Kingdom's main offshore fields, including Safaniyah and Marjan. Saipem announced the awards on 25 November 2026, and fabrication will take place at its yard in Saudi Arabia.

Contract Value and Structure

The two awards are Contract Release Purchase Orders, issued under Saipem's existing Long-Term Agreement with Aramco. Under these framework agreements, Aramco places individual work packages with pre-qualified contractors without a full new tender. That speeds up awards for the steady stream of maintenance and development work on its offshore fields. Saipem said the US$650 million covers engineering, procurement, construction, installation, pipeline and power cable work.
Both contracts are engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) packages. That means Saipem is responsible for the work from design through to installation offshore. Single-contractor EPCI awards reduce the number of interfaces Aramco has to manage. Saipem did not give a schedule for either contract.

CRPO 168 Across Four Fields

The first contract, CRPO 168, covers four production deck manifolds, about 14 km of pipeline between 12 and 16 inches in diameter, and about 24 km of 15 kV power cable. Production deck manifolds are platform structures that gather oil from several wells before it is sent onward. The scope also includes related subsea facilities in the Abu Safah, Safaniyah, Manifa and Berri fields. These fields are among Aramco's most established offshore producing areas.
CRPO 168 also includes onshore work to tie in a drill site at the Manifa field. Safaniyah is widely described as the world's largest offshore oilfield, and Manifa is a major heavy oil development. New manifolds and pipelines in these fields help connect new wells and keep production steady. Spreading the work across four fields under one contract lets Saipem share resources and vessels between sites.

CRPO 170 at Marjan

The second contract, CRPO 170, covers three production deck manifolds, about 25 km of pipeline between 12 and 16 inches in diameter, and about 17 km of 15 kV power cable. The work also includes associated subsea facilities. All of it is at the Marjan field in the northern Gulf. Marjan has been the focus of a large Aramco expansion programme in recent years.
The power cables in both contracts will supply electricity to offshore facilities. Supplying power by cable can reduce the need for gas turbines or diesel generators on platforms, lowering local emissions. Pipeline and cable installation make up a large share of the combined scope. Together the two contracts add about 39 km of pipeline and 41 km of cable to Aramco's offshore network.

Saudi Market Position

Saipem said the awards strengthen its presence in Saudi Arabia and its long relationship with Aramco. It also said they reflect its engineering and project execution capabilities. Saudi Arabia is one of Saipem's most important markets, and Aramco is among its largest clients. Repeat awards under the Long-Term Agreement give Saipem a steady pipeline of offshore work.
In September 2026, Saipem completed the sale of its shallow-water drilling operations in Saudi Arabia. The latest contracts show the company focusing its Saudi business on offshore engineering and construction. Saipem has 17 owned construction vessels and five fabrication yards worldwide. Continued investment by Aramco to sustain offshore oil output is likely to keep demand for this kind of work high.

Canadian Rig Count Slips to 229 as Natural Gas Drilling Continues to Strengthen

November 26, 2026 EnergyNow Media
     
These translations are done via Google Translate
Print 🖨
Canadian drilling activity declined for a second consecutive reporting period as producers reduced oil drilling, although natural gas activity continued to strengthen heading into the winter drilling season.
Canada’s active rig count fell by two to 229 rigs for the reporting period ended November 25 , according to the latest Baker Hughes North America Rig Count Report.

Despite the decline, Canada has 41 more rigs than the 188 operating during the comparable period last year , an increase of approximately 21.8%.
Oil drilling accounted for the reduction.
Canada’s oil rig count declined by four to 155 , while natural gas rigs increased by one to 71 . Miscellaneous rigs also increased by one to three.
The latest figures extend a notable shift in Canada’s drilling mix over the past two reporting periods.
Since November 13, oil drilling has declined from 164 to 155 rigs, while natural gas activity has increased from 67 to 71.
Although oil development remains the primary driver of Canada’s year-over-year drilling expansion, the recent increase in natural gas activity provides an interesting counterpoint.
The shift comes amid continued volatility across global energy markets.

Western Canada’s natural gas industry continues to adapt to additional demand opportunities associated with LNG exports, although regional prices, transportation capacity and production economics remain important factors in drilling decisions.
Despite the recent reduction in oil rigs, Canada’s year-over-year drilling comparisons remain particularly strong.
The country’s 155 oil rigs represent a 28% increase from the 121 operating a year ago , while natural gas activity has increased by approximately 6%, from 67 to 71 rigs.
Canadian offshore activity also strengthened, increasing by one to three rigs, compared with none operating during the comparable period last year.
Onshore activity declined by three to 226 rigs.
The broader recovery from September’s drilling slowdown remains intact.
Canada’s national fleet fell to 197 rigs on September 18 before recovering to 233 by November 13.
At 229 rigs, the country remains approximately 16% above its September low, despite losing four rigs over the past two reporting periods.
For Canadian drilling contractors and oilfield services companies, the substantially stronger year-over-year activity levels remain encouraging as the industry moves into its important winter operating season.
The coming weeks will provide a clearer indication of whether the recent reduction in oil drilling represents a temporary adjustment or the beginning of a more sustained response to weaker crude prices.
For now, Canada continues to operate nearly 22% more rigs than it did a year ago, with natural gas drilling gaining momentum even as oil activity softens.
Source: Baker Hughes North America Rig Count Report, November 25, 2026.
